summary: Lists the documents that specify the official protocols used in the Internet, with comments on revisions or changes planned. It is a status report that replaces RFC 961, RFC 944 and RFC 924, and was replaced by RFC 1011.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a reading list that tells you which rulebooks the Internet officially follows and which ones are about to change.

subtitle: The 1986 reference for official Internet protocols and their status.

tldr.problem: As Internet protocols continued to evolve and expand, the community needed an updated authoritative guide to which protocols were official and how they should be used.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists and describes all official Internet protocols with their status, specifications, known issues, dependencies, and contacts for the 1986 era.
tldr.outcome: It served as the reference for protocol status through late 1986 and was replaced by RFC 1011 as the protocol suite continued to expand with new features like multicast support.

today: RFC 991 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 1011 in May 1987. Modern Internet protocol status is maintained through the IETF standards track and IANA registries.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 991 identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet and is an official status report for the ARPA-Internet community. It obsoletes RFC 961, RFC 944, RFC 924, and earlier protocol status documents.

The RFC notes that the primary reference for official protocols is now the "DDN Protocol Handbook" (DPH) dated December 1985, a three-volume set. Earlier collections including the "Internet Protocol Transition Workbook" (IPTW), "Internet Mail Protocols," "Internet Telnet Protocols and Options," "Internet Protocol Implementers Guide," and the older "ARPANET Protocol Handbook" contained much of this material, now consolidated in the DPH.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a guide to which network rules the Internet officially uses in 1986. It explains which ones are mandatory, recommended, optional, or experimental.

sections.title: Protocol Organization and Status Framework
sections.content:
Protocols are organized by their functional layer: overview/conceptual (Catenet Model), network level (IP and related), host level (UDP, TCP), gateway level (routing protocols), and application level (Telnet, mail, etc.).

Each protocol entry includes consistent information: STATUS indicating the implementation requirement (required, recommended, elective, experimental, or none), SPECIFICATION documents, COMMENTS on issues and changes, OTHER REFERENCES for additional information, DEPENDENCIES on other protocols, and CONTACT information for technical questions.

The status categories reflect how broadly each protocol must or should be implemented. Required protocols must be in every host. Recommended protocols should be in most hosts. Elective protocols are optional. Experimental protocols are for research only and require coordination with the contact person.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol is described with its purpose, status, problems that were found, and who to contact with questions about it.

sections.title: Network Core and Multicast Protocols
sections.content:
Internet Protocol (IP), specified in RFC 791, is required and remains the universal datagram protocol providing host addressing throughout the Internet. RFC 991 notes ongoing confusion in IP route option processing and mentions work underway on security options.

Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), specified in RFC 792, is required and integral to IP. It carries error reports and control messages. The RFC notes that RFC 950 defined two additional ICMP message types: Address Mask Request and Address Mask Reply, extending ICMP functionality.

Internet Group Multicast Protocol (IGMP), specified in RFC 988, is now recommended. It specifies extensions for Internet Protocol host implementation to support internetwork multicasting, enabling one-to-many communication patterns. This represents a significant expansion of Internet communication capabilities since the earlier protocol documents.
sections.plainLanguage: IP moves messages between computers. ICMP reports when something goes wrong. IGMP is new and lets one computer send the same message to many computers at once, which is useful for broadcasting.

sections.title: Host Transport and Application Services
sections.content:
User Datagram Protocol (UDP), specified in RFC 768, is recommended. It provides fast, connectionless datagram service with port-based addressing, useful for applications that do not require guaranteed delivery.

Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), specified in RFC 793, is recommended. It provides reliable, ordered data streams essential for applications requiring data integrity. RFC 991 includes extensive implementation notes addressing window and acknowledgement strategy, event processing, and segment handling.

Telnet Protocol, specified in RFC 854, is recommended for remote interactive terminal access. Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) and associated mail protocols are documented separately. The RFC also references File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and Domain Name System (DNS).

Experimental protocols continue to address specialized needs: Stream Protocol (ST) for real-time resource allocation, Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) for bulk data in high-latency environments, and others for monitoring and specialized transactions.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP is the quick way to send independent messages. TCP is the reliable way to send data that must arrive complete and in order. Telnet, mail, and file transfer are the main applications.

sections.title: Gateway and Experimental Protocols
sections.content:
Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) is recommended for gateways to exchange routing information between different autonomous systems. Gateway Gateway Protocol (GGP) is used experimentally in core Internet gateways for internal routing.

Multiplexing Protocol (MUX) and Stream Protocol (ST) address specialized needs in resource-constrained and real-time environments. Network Voice Protocol (NVP-II) defines procedures for real-time voice conferencing.

Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) is designed for bulk data transfer in environments with long transmission delays and non-sequential delivery. Internet Reliable Transaction Protocol (IRTP) provides transport-level host-to-host communication for specific application patterns.

The RFC emphasizes that experimental protocol use requires coordination with named contacts and should only proceed when participants are actively researching the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateway protocols help routers talk to each other. Experimental protocols are being tested for specialized jobs like voice calls, bulk file transfer over slow connections, and transaction processing.
